title: GUI vs. CLI: Where Computer-Use Agents Get Stuck
hook: Should an agent click buttons or type commands? A matched benchmark giving both the same 440 tasks finds GUI agents win by default — but CLI agents leap ahead once their skill library is filled in.
key_points: Computer-use agents can act through graphical interfaces (clicking) or command-line interfaces (typing commands).
Prior comparisons confound modality with different tasks, states, and verifiers; this work matches all of them across 440 desktop tasks, 18 apps, 12 categories.
The strongest screen-only GUI agent reaches 59.1% full pass vs 48.2% for the strongest original-skill CLI agent.
Adding verifier-guided skill coverage lifts the CLI agent to 69.3% — so most of its deficit was missing skills, not weak reasoning.
Different bottlenecks: GUI agents struggle with reliable grounded interaction over long workflows; CLI agents with skill coverage and scalability.
content_html: When an AI agent operates a computer, it can work like a person — looking at the screen and clicking — or like a developer, issuing commands through a CLI. This paper builds a fair fight between the two and finds the answer is less about modality than about what's been built around each.
extra_html:
A matched benchmark

Past comparisons mixed up the interaction modality with everything else: different tasks, starting states, verifiers, and allowed actions. The authors instead give screen-only GUI agents and skill-mediated CLI agents the same 440 desktop tasks across 18 applications and 12 workflow categories, with identical goals, states, and final-state verifiers — each restricted to its native actions.

The findings

By default the strongest GUI agent wins, hitting a 59.1% full pass rate versus 48.2% for the best original-skill CLI agent. But that gap is misleading: when the CLI agent's skill library is expanded with verifier-guided augmentation, its success jumps to 69.3%, overtaking the GUI agent. The deficit was mostly missing skills, not weaker reasoning. The two modalities expose different failure modes — GUI agents are bottlenecked by reliable grounded interaction over long workflows, while CLI agents are bottlenecked by how completely and scalably their skill interfaces cover the task space.

flashcards.prompt: Why did this benchmark match tasks, states, and verifiers across GUI and CLI agents?
flashcards.back_html: Because earlier comparisons confounded interaction modality with differences in tasks, initial states, verifiers, and permitted actions — so you couldn't tell whether the modality or the setup drove the result.

flashcards.explanation_html: With augmented skills, the CLI agent jumped past the best GUI agent, showing the gap was largely about the coverage and scalability of its skill interface.

flashcards.prompt: What distinct bottleneck limits GUI agents vs CLI agents?
flashcards.back_html: GUI agents are limited by reliable grounded interaction over long-horizon workflows; CLI agents are limited by the coverage and scalability of their skill interfaces.
